newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Bank Austria takes reins at Creditanstalt .
newsitem.headline: Bank Austria takes reins at Creditanstalt .

text.p: Bank Austria AG chief executive Gerhard Randa took the helm at Creditanstalt-Bankverein's supervisory board on Friday, finally clinching full control of the bank that once was his closest competitor.

The vote came shortly after the bank's extraordinary shareholders' meeting elected Randa and two other members of Bank Austria's executive board, Karl Samstag and Friedrich Kadrnoska, onto the supervisory board with more than 99 percent of votes.
Randa, the mastermind behind Austria's biggest corporate takeover since World War Two, replaces Walter Fremuth, who resigned after four years as supervisory board chief.

"I can assure you that I will use all my experience, all my power and all my abilities for the benefit of this institution, its customers, all its staff, and particularly that of its shareholders," Randa, 52, told shareholders.
Eight other candidates presented by Bank Austria for the 21-member council were also voted in with majorities of more than 90 percent.

Bank Austria bought the Austrian government's 69.45 percent voting stake in Creditanstalt in January for 17.2 billion schillings in cash, closing the book on Europe's longest running privatisation saga.
The fate of the bank's executive board, headed by Guido Schmidt-Chiari since 1988, will be decided at the next regular meeting of Creditanstalt's supervisory board on April 29.
Schmidt-Chiari has said he will resign from his post, and Randa is expected to pick a successor with close ties to Bank Austria.

According to the fine print of the takeover, Creditanstalt will remain an independent bank for at least five years. Randa has indicated he wants to keep the Creditanstalt brand name alive alongside that of Bank Austria.
"I see the two brand-name strategy in place for the next five to 10 years," he said last month.

The small shareholders of Creditanstalt will be offered the possibility to exchange their stock for Bank Austria shares. Randa told reporters after the meeting that the exact details of the exchange offer would be put to a shareholder vote at another extraordinary meeeting scheduled for September.
Under the terms of the deal, sanctioned by the Austrian government, shareholders of Creditanstalt will be offered an unspecified number of Bank Austria shares or an 722.5 schilling cash alternative.

The merger of Austria's two top banks has created a financial powerhouse with some 1,300 billion schillings in total assets which controls 70 percent of commercial banking and 80 percent of Vienna bourse trade.
The privatisation of blue-blooded Creditanstalt had caused a deep rift in Austria's government coalition of dominant Social Democrats and conservative People's Party.

An eleventh-hour deal saved the government from collapse, but at a hefty price for the conservatives who lost their key fight to keep conservative stronghold Creditanstalt out of the reach of Social-Democrat dominated Bank Austria.

Bank Austria is effectively controlled by the City of Vienna and 19-percent owned by the Austrian government. According to the deal, the city's stake will be cut to below 20 percent over seven years while the state's stake will be sold this year.
